data.name: Just A Dream
data.detailed_description:
Just a Dream is a fast paced top down action game. You enter a world filled with your worst nightmares and must escape. As you fight across your dream from level to level, you encounter the very things that you dread every night. Pick up unique weapons and use magical abilities that allow you to traverse the lands of nightmares and monsters to conquer Anxiety, Fear, and Despair themselves. Your adventure starts as you must escape back into the realms of reality.

  • 36 unique abilities with thousands of unique combinations
  • 4 different environments, all ending with an intense boss fight, integrated with a unique musical theme for each
  • Randomly generated levels to ensure one never has the same experience
  • Many weapons from the Assault King to the Salt Shotgun
  • Unlock abilities easily and cosmetics for the more adventurous to prove their prowess

All assets were created by our team and a few helpers.

reviews.review:
Just A Dream takes the familiar idea of being trapped inside a nightmare and turns it into a compact top-down action experience centered on survival, experimentation, and repeated attempts. Developed and published by The Hyper Carries!, the game puts players in a surreal struggle against creatures and challenges associated with negative emotions. Rather than presenting its dream setting as a slow psychological horror adventure, it favors immediate combat and arcade-like progression, creating an experience that is easy to understand while still offering enough variation to encourage multiple runs.

The main objective is to navigate procedurally generated levels, defeat enemies, strengthen your character, and survive long enough to confront the major threats waiting deeper within the nightmare. Randomized level generation gives each attempt some unpredictability, particularly in the arrangement of encounters and the route through each area. It does not completely eliminate repetition, since the fundamental combat loop remains consistent, but it prevents the adventure from becoming entirely dependent on memorizing one fixed sequence of rooms. This works particularly well with the dream concept, where instability and uncertainty naturally fit the setting.

Combat is straightforward but gains flexibility through the game's collection of 36 abilities. These abilities represent one of its most substantial gameplay features because they can be combined in different ways, allowing players to experiment with builds rather than following exactly the same strategy every time. Some combinations can improve offensive potential, while others can make movement or survival easier. Finding effective interactions between abilities becomes part of the satisfaction, and unlocking more options gradually expands the possibilities available during subsequent attempts.

Weapons contribute additional variety and demonstrate the game's somewhat playful personality. Equipment such as the Assault King and Salt Shotgun prevents the nightmare theme from becoming excessively serious, giving the action a quirky quality alongside its darker concepts. Switching between weapons can alter how aggressively or cautiously encounters are approached. Although the underlying shooting and action mechanics are not exceptionally complex, combining weapons with different abilities provides enough tactical flexibility to make experimentation worthwhile.

The journey is divided across four environments, with individual musical themes helping distinguish one location from another. Boss encounters serve as major tests along the way, and the game's themes of Anxiety, Fear, and Despair give these confrontations more conceptual meaning than simply fighting increasingly powerful monsters. The story is not presented as an elaborate psychological examination, but there is something appealing about transforming difficult emotions into tangible obstacles that can be fought and eventually overcome.

Bosses also provide some of the game's more demanding moments. Regular enemies can often be handled through aggressive movement and effective use of weapons, whereas bosses encourage players to recognize attack patterns, maintain appropriate positioning, and make better use of their accumulated abilities. Special challenges and achievements extend this further by asking players to accomplish objectives beyond simply reaching the ending. This gives players who enjoy completion hunting an additional layer of goals after becoming comfortable with the standard progression.

Cosmetic rewards further support long-term play. They are not essential to character strength, which is a sensible choice because important gameplay progression remains separate from rewards intended mainly as demonstrations of accomplishment. Players interested only in completing the main experience can concentrate on abilities, weapons, and bosses, while dedicated players can pursue additional objectives and cosmetic unlocks. Combined with the procedural structure, these optional challenges give a relatively small game more replay value than its initial scope might suggest.

Visually, Just A Dream is clearly a modest independent production rather than a showcase for advanced graphics. Its presentation prioritizes readability and functional action over elaborate environmental detail. The surreal nightmare premise works in its favor because strange enemies and environments do not need to obey realistic rules. The individual music associated with environments and major encounters also helps provide atmosphere. Greater visual and enemy variety would have made repeated runs feel fresher, but the existing presentation supports the gameplay effectively.

Its biggest limitation is overall depth. Players familiar with large modern roguelikes and roguelites may expect enormous item pools, complicated character builds, extensive permanent progression, branching routes, or hundreds of hours of meaningful variation. Just A Dream operates on a considerably smaller scale. Once its major weapons, abilities, environments, and enemy behaviors become familiar, repetition becomes more noticeable. The procedural generation helps, but randomized layouts cannot entirely replace additional mechanical and content variety. The game is consequently best approached as a focused arcade action experience rather than an endlessly expandable roguelike.

Steam Deck compatibility should be considered unverified rather than officially supported. The game does not have an official Steam Deck Verified or Playable designation, so there is no guarantee that every aspect will function correctly on Valve's handheld. Its relatively lightweight presentation and straightforward gameplay could potentially make it suitable for handheld play through compatibility tools, but players should not interpret that possibility as confirmed support. Controller behavior, interface usability, performance, and compatibility may therefore require individual testing.

Taken as a whole, Just A Dream is an interesting small-scale action game that makes good use of its nightmare concept. Its 36 abilities, unusual weapons, randomized stages, four environments, bosses, achievements, and cosmetic rewards provide a respectable collection of systems without making the experience unnecessarily complicated. The repetitive nature of its combat and limited overall scope keep it from competing with deeper genre leaders, but its accessible structure makes it easy to pick up and experiment with. For players who enjoy top-down action, procedural stages, ability combinations, achievement hunting, and unusual indie projects, there is enough personality here to make escaping this particular nightmare worth attempting.

Rating: 7/10
